chunks.section: Subspace Crystallization in Grokking: Rank Compression Tracks the Phase Transition
chunks.text: Shlok Mehendale † † thanks: Corresponding author: shlok.mehendale@lossfunk.com Affiliation: Lossfunk Paras Chopra Affiliation: Lossfunk

Grokking describes understanding something deeply and intuitively. In neural networks, it is the phenomenon where a network generalizes long after memorizing its training data. This delay has been linked to a fall in the effective rank of the network’s weight matrices, but whether this rank compression drives grokking or follows it is still unresolved. We study a mean-field MLP and a one-layer transformer trained on modular arithmetic and observe that: (i) Compression follows the onset, not memorization. Every transformer memorizes its training data within 250 steps, while the grokking onset (the first step at which test accuracy reaches 95%) varies from 6,500 to 21,000 steps. The steepest fall in effective rank comes about 900 steps after the onset, however late the onset occurs, and networks that memorize without grokking compress far less. (ii) Subspace crystallization. We call the span of the fewest top singular directions of a weight matrix that preserve 99% of test accuracy its sufficient subspace . Its size can shrink as the margin between the correct and the best wrong output grows, so we also count the directions needed to keep the outputs within 10%. In the transformer, this count falls during the transition from a quarter or more of the available directions to about a tenth, which we call subspace crystallization . (iii) Imposing low rank does not speed up grokking. Against a factorized full-rank control, capping the rank of the transformer’s MLP input weights delays the onset, and capping the rank of its embedding stops 15 of 20 runs from grokking. Compression is therefore a signature of grokking rather than its cause.

Grokking ( Power et al., 2022 ) , memorization followed by delayed generalization, offers a rare window into how circuits emerge from gradient descent: a clean phase transition from a lazy, memorizing regime to a rich, generalizing one ( Kumar et al., 2024 ) . Substantial progress exists on what grokking networks compute ( Nanda et al., 2023 ; Chughtai et al., 2023 ; Gromov, 2023 ) , and a recurring observation is that the effective rank (ER) of their weight matrices falls as test accuracy jumps ( Liu et al., 2023b ; DeMoss et al., 2025 ; Lei and Xu, 2026 ) . This has led to proposals that a pressure toward low-rank, small-norm or efficient circuits causes grokking ( Nanda et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023a ; Varma et al., 2023 ) . We ask two questions. (Q1) Does this rank compression cause grokking, or follow it? (Q2) Does the learned solution lie in the subspace spanned by a few leading directions of each weight matrix?

The usual evidence cannot settle these questions, for three reasons. First, rank compression is usually observed after two events, memorization (the first step at which training accuracy reaches 99%) and the rise in test accuracy (Figure 1 a), so the timing alone cannot explain which of the two it follows. Second, timing without interventions cannot show cause. Lastly, the compactness of a solution is naturally measured by truncating each weight matrix to lower and lower rank until test accuracy drops. Keeping a weight matrix’s k k strongest singular directions gives the closest rank- k k matrix, which acts only within their span. The span of the fewest top directions that leave the test accuracy unchanged, which we call the sufficient subspace , is then taken as the subspace the solution needs, analogous to the intrinsic dimension of Li et al. (2018) . Accuracy, however, only checks which output is largest. The margin between the correct-class output and the largest other output sets how far the outputs can move before a prediction changes. As margins grow, more directions can be deleted before any prediction changes, so the count can fall even though the network’s outputs still depend on those directions.

We address these questions with geometric metrics (effective rank, stable rank, sparsity, inverse participation ratio) and multiple interventions (truncation of weight matrices to their top, bottom or random singular directions, complement interventions, transplant patching with orthogonal alignment, a nuclear-norm penalty, rank caps compared with factorized controls, and optimizer swaps). In the transformer, we analyze the embedding W E W_{E} , the unembedding W U W_{U} , and the input and output matrices W in W_{\text{in}} and W out W_{\text{out}} of its MLP block. We call the first step at which test accuracy reaches 95% the grokking onset . To separate memorization from the onset, we follow the transformer with a checkpoint every 250 steps and compare networks that grok with networks that memorize but never grok. To count directions without the margin, we judge each truncation by how much it changes the network’s outputs. To test cause, we limit the rank of a weight matrix throughout training and compare each limit with a factorized full-rank control. • Compression follows grokking, not memorization (§ 6 ). Every transformer memorizes its training data within 250 steps, but the steepest fall in the effective rank of W in W_{\text{in}} comes about 900 steps after the grokking onset, whether the onset occurs at step 6,500 or 21,000. Networks that memorize without grokking lower this effective rank by 15–23%, against 60 ± 5 % 60\pm 5\% in those that grok. In the MLP, rank compression follows the onset in all 45 runs across three tasks. The timing replicates on 15 held-out seeds and, in the MLP, on two further tasks. • Subspace crystallization: the transformer’s solution narrows to a low-dimensional subspace (§ 5 , § 7 ). Before the transition, no weight matrix can be truncated below 27–53 directions without changing the network’s outputs by more than 10%. After the transition, 8–13 directions suffice (Figure 1 b). We call this narrowing of the subspace that the outputs depend on subspace crystallization . It is consistent with the removal of memorizing components described by Nanda et al. (2023) . We judge truncations by the outputs rather than only by the test accuracy. In the MLP trained with mean-squared error, truncation to 65 of 128 directions keeps the test accuracy, but keeping the outputs within 10% needs 122–127.

• Imposing low rank before the transition does not speed up grokking (§ 6.4 ). If rank compression drove grokking, removing directions in advance should help. Instead, against a factorized full-rank control, capping W in W_{\text{in}} at rank 32, 24 or 16, all above the 13 directions its solution needs, never lowers the mean onset, and capping W E W_{E} prevents grokking in 15 of 20 runs. Compressing the MLP’s first layer with a nuclear-norm penalty before the onset also delays grokking, and comparing with the unfactorized network instead of the factorized control would wrongly suggest that low rank speeds grokking up, because the factorization changes the onset by itself. We also report three secondary results. The late fall of effective rank in the MLP is set by AdamW’s ϵ \epsilon : once the square root of its second-moment estimate falls below ϵ \epsilon , its updates reduce to gradient descent with momentum and learning rate lr / ϵ \text{lr}/\epsilon (§ 4 ). Different MLP seeds share their hidden representation up to an orthogonal rotation, but not with networks trained on another task or on random labels (§ 5 ). The Fourier inverse participation ratio (IPR), which measures how periodic the hidden units are ( Doshi et al., 2024 ) , rises before the onset but also in every network that never groks, so it cannot serve as a label-free early-warning signal (§ 6.5 ). Table 1 summarizes the evidence for the three contributions in both architectures.

Grokking was given its first mechanistic account by Nanda et al. (2023) , who identified the learned algorithm as a sparse Fourier cosine decomposition, formed in phases of memorization, circuit formation and cleanup. Chughtai et al. (2023) extended this to general group composition, and Gromov (2023) established exact solvability with analytic weights. Proposed causes of the delay include circuit efficiency ( Varma et al., 2023 ) , the weight norm ( Liu et al., 2023a ) , softmax collapse ( Prieto et al., 2025 ) and a transition from lazy to rich training ( Kumar et al., 2024 ) . Lei and Xu (2026) describe grokking as construction followed by compression, tracked through the network’s Jacobian, consistent with our timing results. We add the separation of compression from memorization, negative controls and a replication on held-out seeds and tasks. Musat (2025) proves that, in the limit of small learning rate and weight decay, gradient descent after memorization minimizes the weight norm on the zero-loss manifold. Our MLP lies outside this regime: late in training, AdamW acts as gradient descent with a large learning rate lr / ϵ = 10 5 \text{lr}/\epsilon=10^{5} , and the weight norm grows (§ 4 ).

Network complexity falls around the accuracy jump, whether measured by the linear mapping number ( Liu et al., 2023b ) or by the compressed description length of the weights ( DeMoss et al., 2025 ) . We test whether this fall drives grokking or follows it, and show that a count of directions judged by accuracy can register compression that the network’s outputs do not show (§ 5 ). Gradient descent is biased toward low-rank solutions ( Huh et al., 2023 ) and moves within a small subspace of parameter space ( Gur-Ari et al., 2018 ) . Factorizing a matrix strengthens this bias ( Arora et al., 2019 ) and accelerates optimization ( Arora et al., 2018 ) , so a rank cap written as a product W = A ​ B W=AB changes the optimization as well as the rank. We therefore compare each cap with a factorized full-rank control (§ 6.4 ).

Merrill et al. (2023) describe grokking as a competition between a sparse generalizing subnetwork and a dense memorizing one, consistent with the few directions per matrix that the transformer’s solution keeps. Networks trained on modular arithmetic can learn different algorithms ( Zhong et al., 2023 ) or share one across architectures ( Chughtai et al., 2023 ) . Our MLP seeds use different Fourier coordinates but share their hidden representation up to a rotation (§ 5 ). Appendix A discusses further work.

chunks.section: Stage 4 is set by the effective learning rate.
chunks.text: Stage 4 is growth of the leading singular directions of W 1 W_{1} against weight decay: between steps 20,000 and 10 5 10^{5} the largest singular value doubles (112 to 218) while the remaining 63 directions keep their size (Appendix C.1 ). The loss gradient that drives this growth is tiny ( 3.4 × 10 − 6 3.4\times 10^{-6} at step 20,000), points increasingly outward along the weights (its cosine with − θ -\theta rises from 0.19 to 0.89) and concentrates in the top 65 directions of W 1 W_{1} (from 43% to 87% of its squared norm). For 87–100% of the coordinates, the square root of Adam’s second-moment estimate lies below ϵ \epsilon , so the update m / ( v + ϵ ) m/(\sqrt{v}+\epsilon) is close to m / ϵ m/\epsilon : AdamW acts as gradient descent with learning rate lr / ϵ = 10 5 \text{lr}/\epsilon=10^{5} (Appendix C.2 ). Continuing the main runs from step 20,000 with other optimizers confirms that this effective learning rate, not Adam itself, governs Stage 4 (Table 2 ). At effective learning rates of 10 3 10^{3} and 10 4 10^{4} , AdamW and gradient descent reach the same weights. At 10 5 10^{5} , gradient descent reproduces most of Stage 4 and SGD with momentum reproduces all of it (effective rank 108.3 108.3 and 103.8 103.8 , against 104.8 104.8 under AdamW). At 10 3 10^{3} , weight decay shrinks the norm and effective rank stays at 117.8, while ϵ ≤ 10 − 9 \epsilon\leq 10^{-9} strengthens Stage 4.

Each seed thus implements the same task-relevant representation in a different orientation, consistent with Schiffman (2026) , who find invariant algorithmic cores in independently trained transformers.

We test whether compression drives grokking with three kinds of evidence: its timing across seeds, how much the effective rank decreases in networks that memorize without grokking, and interventions that impose low rank from initialization.

chunks.section: 6.1 Compression Follows the Onset, Not Memorization
chunks.text: The transformer separates memorization from the transition, and compression follows the transition. Every one of the 29 grokked seeds (seeds 0–14 and the held-out seeds 15–29) fits its training set within the first 250 steps, while their onsets range from 6,500 to 21,000 steps. With weight decay 1.0, AdamW multiplies the weights by 0.999 per step, so by step 4,000 the initial weights have decayed to 2% of their size. Because random weights spread over all directions, this decay alone lowers the effective rank of W in W_{\text{in}} , to a plateau at about 60% of its initial value, independently of grokking (Figure 9 ). We therefore measure compression only after step 4,000. After this decay, a second, sharp drop follows. The step t s t_{s} at which this second drop is steepest follows the onset almost exactly (Pearson correlation r = 0.99 r=0.99 , slope 1.02 1.02 , 95% confidence interval 0.98 0.98 – 1.07 1.07 ), scattering by 506 steps around t g t_{g} against 4,234 around the memorization step (Figure 1(a) ). If compression followed memorization, t s t_{s} would cluster at a fixed step.

chunks.section: 6.1 Compression Follows the Onset, Not Memorization
chunks.text: Networks that memorize without grokking compress far less. From step 4,000 to the end of training, the ER of W in W_{\text{in}} falls by 60 ± 5 % 60\pm 5\% in grokked transformers but by only 15–23% in the seven that never grok, at a peak rate two to five times lower (Appendix E.2 ). In the MLP, whose onset and memorization time barely vary across seeds, the random-label networks reach 90% training accuracy without grokking, and their effective rank falls by 1.1 ± 0.3 % 1.1\pm 0.3\% , against 10.5 ± 1.8 % 10.5\pm 1.8\% in grokked MLPs. Comparing seeds at the same training step shows that low rank is acquired at the transition itself (Appendix Table 21 ): before their own onset, grokked seeds have as many directions as the seed that never groks, and after it far fewer.

chunks.section: 6.2 Compression Does Not Start Before the Rise in Test Accuracy

All 15 seeds have t c > t g t_{c}>t_{g} , with mean lag 6,367 ± 3,248 6{,}367\pm 3{,}248 steps (one-sided t = 7.59 t=7.59 , p = 1.3 × 10 − 6 p=1.3\times 10^{-6} ), i.e. 50 ± 25 % 50\pm 25\% of t g t_{g} . Granger tests agree: changes in test accuracy predict changes in effective rank in all 15 seeds, and the reverse holds in at most 6 (Appendix E.1 ). In the transformer, compression is part of the transition. We locate the start t on t_{\text{on}} of the second drop as the first step of the stretch leading up to t s t_{s} in which the decrease is at least 20% of its peak rate, using a centered five-point moving average that adds no delay (Appendix E.1 ). The drop starts 1,888 ± 992 1{,}888\pm 992 steps before the onset, but after test accuracy has first reached 10% in 28 of 29 seeds (median 1,750 steps after), at 34 ± 22 % 34\pm 22\% test accuracy. It is steepest 905 ± 506 905\pm 506 steps after the onset (27 of 29 seeds), and 63% of it happens after the onset. In both architectures, then, compression does not start before test accuracy begins to rise. In the MLP it starts after the transition, and in the transformer during it.

We tested the timing results on seeds and tasks not used to define the measures, and report every test (Table 22 ). On the 15 held-out transformer seeds (H1), the steepest decrease came 850 ± 524 850\pm 524 steps after the onset (14 of 15 seeds, the fifteenth at the onset, one-sided t = 6.28 t=6.28 , p = 1.0 × 10 − 5 p=1.0\times 10^{-5} ), close to the 964 ± 499 964\pm 499 steps of seeds 0–14, on which the measure had been defined. chunks.section: 8 Why the Transformer Crystallizes Further Than the MLP
chunks.text: We attribute this gap to the architecture. The transformer’s embedding uses about four frequencies: 4.2 ± 0.7 4.2\pm 0.7 of them hold 90% of its Fourier power. Each frequency requires two directions, a cosine and a sine, so this predicts about 8 directions, close to d 0.99 d_{0.99} of W E W_{E} , W out W_{\text{out}} and W U W_{U} (7.7–8.8, Table 31 ). The directions attention writes to nearly coincide with those W in W_{\text{in}} reads from (mean cosine of the principal angles 0.923 0.923 , against 0.248 0.248 for random subspaces), and equally so in runs that never grok (Appendix F ). The MLP block therefore receives an input already confined to a few directions, and the directions its outputs do not need are removed during the transition, together with the memorizing components (§ 7 ). The MLP’s first layer instead reads both one-hot operands directly, so each frequency costs it four directions, and it spreads its weights over most of the 48 frequencies (§ 5 ). No MLP we trained crystallizes during the transition.

chunks.section: 8 Why the Transformer Crystallizes Further Than the MLP
chunks.text: Other differences between the models, i.e. loss and the weight decay do not account for the gap. The loss explains only why the cross-entropy MLP ends with fewer representative directions than the mean-squared-error MLP. A one-hot target has equal power at all 97 Fourier components, so for a network that matches its targets, omitting one frequency changes the outputs by 2 / 97 ≈ 14 % \sqrt{2/97}\approx 14\% , more than d out d_{\text{out}} allows. CE constrains only the ordering of the logits, and the CE MLP ends at d out d_{\text{out}} = 70–81, against 122–127 with MSE. Raising its weight decay to the transformer’s per-step shrinkage of 10 − 3 10^{-3} speeds up grokking, from step 10,100 10{,}100 to 2,300 2{,}300 , but does not make it crystallize: d out d_{\text{out}} is about 120 just after the onset and ends at 118.4 instead of 69.6, and stronger decay prevents learning (Table 7 ). Only the CE MLP’s d out d_{\text{out}} falls late, and its Stage-4 fall in effective rank is four times as large ( 37.9 % 37.9\% against 9.7 % 9.7\% , Table 6 ), which suggested that the late fall is Stage 4 itself (§ 4 ). Consistently, at every weight decay d out d_{\text{out}} ends close to the effective rank of W 1 W_{1} (69.6 against 71.1, 100.4 against 98.7, 118.4 against 115.7). The cross-entropy MLP’s late narrowing is thus a different process from the transformer’s crystallization.

chunks.section: What our measurements imply for rank analyses.
chunks.text: Our results suggest four practices for measuring how many directions a network uses. First, count directions with a criterion that is independent of the margin, such as d out d_{\text{out}} , and compare the count with that of untrained or memorizing networks: in our MLP, d 0.99 d_{0.99} reported a narrowing that the outputs did not undergo. Second, report the training step with every count: the MLP’s d 0.99 d_{0.99} grows from 65 to 89 after generalization, so it is not a fixed property of the trained model. Third, compare any intervention that imposes low rank with a control of the same parameterization: against the unfactorized MLP, rank caps would wrongly appear to accelerate grokking. Fourth, read weight-spectrum statistics such as IPR or effective rank as signals of grokking only next to negative controls, since they also move in networks that never grok. In the transformer, a few leading singular directions of each matrix carry the solution and truncating to them keeps the test accuracy, while random truncations of equal rank do not (Table 15 , subject to the assumptions in Appendix D.3 ). In the MLP, one seed’s hidden representation transfers to another after an orthogonal alignment fitted on its few thousand training inputs, although their weight subspaces overlap no more than random ones (§ 5 ).

Our tasks are all modular arithmetic on cyclic groups, so a non-abelian group ( Chughtai et al., 2023 ) would test the timing results more broadly. Whether language or vision models have a comparably clean sufficient subspace is a natural next question. Kaushik et al. (2025a) ; Kaushik et al. (2025b) study low-dimensional weight subspaces in such models. Within our setting, the two architectures differ in more than their structure: they are also trained with different losses and for different lengths. We varied weight decay separately and found that it does not explain the difference in crystallization (Appendix B.3 ), but the cross-entropy MLPs need larger learning rates than the mean-squared-error ones to grok within 10 5 10^{5} steps (one of five seeds groks at 10 − 3 10^{-3} ). Finally, the Granger tests capture only temporal order, so our causal conclusions rest on the rank interventions.

We asked whether rank compression causes grokking (Q1) and whether the learned solution comes to lie in a few directions of each weight matrix (Q2). For Q1, compression follows the grokking onset rather than memorization: it tracks the onset across a threefold range of onset times while the training set is memorized within 250 steps, it does not start before test accuracy rises, and forcing low rank from initialization does not bring grokking forward. Compression is therefore a signature of grokking rather than its cause. For Q2, the answer depends on how directions are counted. Judged by the outputs, the transformer crystallizes during the transition, to 8–13 directions per matrix, at the same time as its memorizing components are removed. The MLP trained with mean-squared error does not: its d 0.99 d_{0.99} narrows only because its margins grow, and its late compression tracks the optimizer’s effective learning rate. Counting directions by the outputs rather than by accuracy, and comparing any imposed low rank with a control of the same parameterization, is what makes these distinctions visible.

Grokking also occurs for adversarial robustness [ Humayun et al., 2024 ] , in multi-hop reasoning [ Abramov et al., 2025 ] and in Recursive Feature Machines [ Mallinar et al., 2025 ] . Walker et al. Lyu et al. [2024] prove that homogeneous networks with large initialization and small weight decay move from kernel-like dynamics early in training to a max-margin solution late in training, and Mohamadi et al. [2023] show that a margin-maximization bias explains grokking in two-layer quadratic networks on modular arithmetic, with sample complexity O ~ ​ ( p 5 / 3 ) \tilde{O}(p^{5/3}) against O ⁡ ( p 2 ) O(p^{2}) for kernel methods. [2024] show that Fourier features and irreducible representations emerge from implicit margin maximization, consistent with the Fourier structure our networks learn without any spectral penalty.

Li et al. [2018] train networks in low-dimensional random subspaces of parameter space, and Yunis et al. [2024] relate rank minimization, weight alignment and weight decay beyond grokking. Raghu et al. [2017] compare representations across networks with SVCCA, and our cross-seed results extend this comparison to grokking: the representations differ in raw coordinates and agree up to rotation. Sparse autoencoders [ Bricken et al., 2023 , Cunningham et al., 2024 ] decompose representations into features, a basis complementary to the singular directions used here.

Equating high-variance singular directions with functional relevance assumes that those directions carry the computation rather than optimizer noise, representation drift or dense isotropic features. It also assumes linear, orthogonal structure, which can obscure sparse features stored in non-orthogonal superposition or on nonlinear manifolds. The controls of Table 15 test the first assumption in our setting: the high-variance singular directions carry the computation, while random subspaces of equal rank do not. In the MLP the distinction is weaker, because the sufficient subspace spans most of the directions.

The steepest decrease used in Section 6 is the step of the most negative central-difference derivative of the effective rank after a centered moving average over five logged steps ( np.convolve in same mode, then np.gradient ). Each smoothed value belongs to the logged step at its center, so the smoothing adds no delay. The zero-padded average distorts the last two logged steps and the central difference a third, so we exclude the last four. On synthetic signals the measure places a ramp exactly and a sharp step two logging intervals early (Figure 10 ), so any bias shortens the measured lag. Granger causality [ Granger, 1969 ] tests whether the past of one time series improves the prediction of another beyond that series’ own past. It measures temporal predictive asymmetry, not interventional causation. We use the first differences of effective rank and test accuracy, logged every 500 steps, with lag order L ≤ 4 L\leq 4 chosen by the Akaike information criterion. Augmented Dickey–Fuller tests find these differences stationary in only 8 and 13 of 15 seeds, so we repeat the test after differencing further until the series are stationary in every seed. Changes in test accuracy predict changes in effective rank in every seed in both versions, and the reverse holds in at most 6 of 15 (Table 19 ).
